_doc: HAND-ADJUDICATED OVERRIDES on the automated trim (David 2026-09-12: 'you looked
at all the lines that were cut to make sure we did not lose any good chess
teachings?' then 'i think best if you just go through one by one and do this
Every one of the 148 passages the trim changed was read individually. 133 were
correct. The 15 below were not, and each carries the exact text I approved in
place of what the classifier proposed. `keep` restores the original untouched;
`text` is a hand-written replacement that removes only the chatter and leaves
The recurring failure the classifier makes, and the reason this file exists: a
cut-class pattern condemns the WHOLE clause it matches, so a clause that is one
chess fact glued to one piece of chatter loses both. 'the Alapin, against a very
strong 2198' loses the opening's name to kill the rating. No regex fixes that

overrides.why: The cut line is the LEAD-IN that introduces the recovery-principle list right behind it. Remove it and the list starts cold on 'Complicate - pose your opponent decision after decision'. The list is the best teaching in the file.
overrides.was: We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.

overrides.text: This is the Jobava London — Bf4 paired with Nc3, a cross between the Veresov and the London.
overrides.why: priorVid matched 'my main opening' and took the system's whole definition with it. Bf4+Nc3 and the Veresov/London parentage are the content.
overrides.was: This is the Jobava London — Bf4 paired with Nc3, a cross between the Veresov and the London, and my main opening.

overrides.text: White develops the knight to f3. As a gateway Sicilian for improving players the accelerated dragon is the recommendation.
overrides.why: Which Sicilian suits an improver is real repertoire teaching. Only 'nearing the top of the run' is session chatter.
overrides.was: White develops the knight to f3. As a gateway Sicilian for improving players the accelerated dragon is the recommendation, but nearing the top of the run we reach for the Sicilian we know best.

overrides.text: The pawn to e4, c5 — the Alapin.
overrides.why: The rating cut took the opening's NAME with it.
overrides.was: The pawn to e4, c5 — the Alapin, against a very strong 2198, our strongest opponent to date.

overrides.text: The pawn to e4, c5 — the Alapin Sicilian.
overrides.why: Same shape: 'our favorite' is chatter, 'the Alapin Sicilian' is the opening.
overrides.was: The pawn to e4, c5 — our favorite Alapin Sicilian.

overrides.why: Same shape: 'which we've seen a lot' is chatter, 'the Philidor' names the defence.
overrides.was: Black plays d6 — the Philidor, which we've seen a lot.

overrides.why: Silencing this left the ply with no narration at all. The move survives; the author's surprise at it does not.
overrides.was: The queen to d2 is a move I honestly hadn't come across.

overrides.text: The queen to a5 — it might be inaccurate, because it walks into a lot of tactics. The queen to a5 doesn't do anything immediately, but it pressures the a2-pawn, which is annoying, because we don't want our knight to be the only piece standing between us and checkmate — we want to be safer than that.
overrides.why: 'very impressive play so far' is the chatter; 'it might be inaccurate, because it walks into a lot of tactics' is the verdict on the move just played.
overrides.was: The queen to a5 — very impressive play so far, but it might be inaccurate, because it walks into a lot of tactics. The queen to a5 doesn't do anything immediately, but it pressures the a2-pawn, which is annoying, because we don't want our knight to be the only piece standing between us and checkmate — we want to be safer than that.

overrides.text: Black strikes with the pawn to c5. The normal move now is c3.
overrides.why: 'The normal move now is c3' is theory. Only 'but we've been playing this differently' refers to the run.
overrides.was: Black strikes with the pawn to c5. The normal move now is c3, but we've been playing this differently.

overrides.text: The queen to a3 isn't challenging at all. The critical way — the line the theory recommends — is the queen takes c3, a genuine queen sacrifice; the point is Black is grabbing pieces to justify parting with the queen.
overrides.why: The reason behind the queen sac is the whole lesson. Only 'I'll show you how that goes after the game' is the unkeepable promise.
overrides.was: The queen to a3 isn't challenging at all. The critical way — the line the theory recommends — is the queen takes c3, a genuine queen sacrifice; I'll show you how that goes after the game, but the point is Black is grabbing pieces to justify parting with the queen.

overrides.why: Lead-in again — it ends on a dash and hands off to the next beat. Cutting it orphans that beat's opening.
overrides.was: e5, the knight to d7, and the rook to e1. This game is famous because Fischer shows, in vivid, textbook fashion —

overrides.text: We finally develop the light-squared bishop to g4. White's h4 is stronger than it first looks.
overrides.why: A present-tense judgement of a move on the board. 'Honest admission' and 'this was underestimated' are the author's framing around it.
overrides.was: We finally develop the light-squared bishop to g4. Honest admission: White's h4 is stronger than it first looks — this was underestimated.

overrides.why: Names the CENTER FORK TRICK and the move that avoids it. A named tactical motif is teaching even when it arrives as hindsight.
overrides.was: It's been played a fair amount, but a bishop to c4 is a follow-up mistake that puts White in huge trouble — he should have played a bishop to e2 to avoid the center fork trick.

overrides.why: 'White is judged a touch better, but it's rich and double-edged' evaluates the position in front of the student. 'judged' tripped the past-game class.
overrides.was: There's a known plan here of Qg4, provoking a kingside weakness before dropping back to e2. White is judged a touch better, but it's rich and double-edged. My idea was Qe2 followed by Be3 to trade off that strong dark-squared bishop — and, going for broke, the engine's wild suggestion of castling queenside.

overrides.text: The bishop to b6, the rook to g1, the knight to c4 with check — and we also win the exchange.
overrides.why: The resignation goes; winning the exchange is the point of the line.
overrides.was: The bishop to b6, the rook to g1, the knight to c4 with check — he resigns, and we also win the exchange.
